content: Kidney damage can occur when taking dicloxacillin. Dicloxacillin can also cause blood disorders, including eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, leukopenia, and bone marrow depression. Stop using dicloxacillin and seek medical attention immediately if you experience symptoms such as fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual weakness or tiredness, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, headache, or an abnormal or rapid heartbeat. Liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity, is another potential side effect of dicloxacillin. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience nausea, vomiting, stomach or abdominal pain, fever, weakness, unusual fatigue, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stools, dark-colored urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Certain individuals should not use dicloxacillin, including those allergic to dicloxacillin or any of its ingredients. Your pharmacist can provide a list of ingredients in the specific product you are prescribed. Always take dicloxacillin as directed by your healthcare provider and do not share it with others, even if they have similar symptoms, as it may harm them. Keep this medication out of reach of children. Before using dicloxacillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are taking. This will help determine if dicloxacillin is appropriate for you. Dicloxacillin passes into breast milk, so discuss this with your provider if you are nursing. Dicloxacillin is best absorbed on an empty stomach. Take it with a large glass of water (at least 4 ounces or 120 milliliters) at least one hour before or two hours after meals. Avoid taking it while lying down or just before bedtime. It is unknown if alcohol affects dicloxacillin, but heavy drinking can weaken your immune response and make it harder for your body to fight infections. Always inform your healthcare provider about any other medications you are taking, including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or supplements, as dicloxacillin may interact with other substances. Specific interactions to discuss include tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline, minocycline), probenecid (used for gout), and warfarin (a blood thinner). Avoid taking additional medications, such as antacids or laxatives, without consulting your provider. If you accidentally take too much dicloxacillin, seek medical help immediately by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take double or extra doses. Complete the full course of treatment as prescribed, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of antibiotic resistance. Dicloxacillin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections caused by certain bacteria. It is not effective against viral infections, such as the common cold, influenza, or coronavirus, or non-bacterial infections. Some bacteria may be resistant to dicloxacillin, making it less effective. Your healthcare provider may also prescribe dicloxacillin for other conditions as needed. Dicloxacillin works by killing bacteria by preventing them from forming their cell walls. It is available in 250 mg and 500 mg oral capsules. Store dicloxacillin at room temperature (68°F to 77°F or 20°C to 25°C) and protect it from extreme temperatures. The most common side effects of dicloxacillin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a black hairy tongue. Contact your healthcare provider if these side effects bother you. Serious side effects, while less common, include severe allergic reactions, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, seizures, kidney damage, blood disorders, and liver damage. Seek immediate medical attention if you experience symptoms of these conditions.
